reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Linear erosions or ulcers on the gastric mucosal folds at the level of the diaphragmatic hiatus, occurring within a hiatus hernia
A recognised and frequently overlooked cause of chronic iron-deficiency anaemia and obscure or occult gastrointestinal bleeding
Larger hiatus hernias are more likely to harbour these lesions
Thought to result from mechanical trauma from diaphragmatic movement together with acid injury and local mucosal ischaemia
Often asymptomatic, being discovered during endoscopy for anaemia, though they can occasionally cause acute overt bleeding
Easily missed at endoscopy unless the hernia sac is carefully inspected on both forward and retroflexed views
Managed with acid suppression and iron replacement, with surgical hernia repair reserved for refractory or recurrent bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: Cameron lesions are linear erosions or ulcers that develop on the crests of gastric folds where they are compressed by the diaphragmatic hiatus within a hiatus hernia. Their formation is attributed to a combination of mechanical trauma from repetitive movement of the herniated stomach against the diaphragm, chronic acid exposure, and localised mucosal ischaemia at the point of constriction. The resulting slow, repetitive blood loss commonly manifests as iron-deficiency anaemia, and the risk increases with the size of the hernia.
additionalDifferentials: Coeliac disease or other small-bowel causes of iron-deficiency anaemia
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with careful inspection of the hernia sac, including retroflexion, to identify the linear erosions
Full blood count and iron studies to characterise the anaemia
Faecal occult blood testing where occult loss is suspected
Repeat or second-look endoscopy if initial examination is negative but suspicion remains
Evaluation of the remainder of the gastrointestinal tract to exclude a second source of bleeding
Cross-sectional imaging or contrast study to define the size of the hiatus hernia
redFlags: Acute overt gastrointestinal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
Transfusion-dependent or recurrent anaemia despite medical therapy
A large or complex hiatus hernia with strangulation risk
Failure of anaemia to correct on iron and acid suppression
reference.prognosis: Most cases respond well to acid suppression and iron replacement with resolution of anaemia, and surgical repair of the hiatus hernia is effective for the minority with refractory or recurrent bleeding.
pitfalls: Missing the lesions by not carefully examining and retroflexing within the hernia sac
Attributing iron-deficiency anaemia to another cause and overlooking the hernia
Assuming absence of symptoms excludes clinically important blood loss
Not considering surgical repair when bleeding recurs despite medical treatment
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Suppress acid with a proton pump inhibitor to promote healing of the linear erosions
Correct iron-deficiency anaemia with oral or intravenous iron replacement
Achieve endoscopic haemostasis and transfuse where a lesion causes acute overt bleeding
Search for and exclude a coexisting second source of gastrointestinal blood loss
Monitor haemoglobin and iron studies to confirm resolution of the anaemia
Refer for surgical repair of the hiatus hernia, such as fundoplication, in refractory or recurrent bleeding
